title: The Screen That Ate Your Child's Education Classroom Practice (larrycuban.wordpress.com), November 16, 2025 https://larrycuban.wordpress.com/2025/12/03/the-screen-that-ate-your-childs-education-jean-twenge/
author: Jean Twenge
source: The New York Times (nytimes.com); republished at Larry Cuban on School Reform and
summary: Jean Twenge argues that the decline in American and global student test scores, which began around 2012 -- well before the pandemic -- is significantly linked to electronic device use in schools, and that the culprit is broader than smartphones alone: school-issued laptops and tablets are doing comparable damage. She cites concrete cases, including a Washington, D.C. ninth-grader who spent entire class periods watching TV and playing games on a school-issued laptop, and a Common Sense Media survey in which a quarter of teens reported seeing pornographic content during the school day, nearly half of them on a school device. Twenge marshals research showing college students who multitask on laptops during class score lower on exams even controlling for academic ability, a 2023 UNESCO report linking device use to poorer academic performance internationally, and her own October study in the Journal of Adolescence finding countries where students use devices more for leisure during school hours show sharper test-score declines -- with Finland's plunge and Japan's relative stability offered as a natural contrast. She closes with concrete policy recommendations: lock down school devices more securely, give teachers district-wide backing to restrict non-educational use, scale back assignments that require a device, let parents opt out of school-issued devices, and consider device-free models in lower grades.
points: Twenge's core evidentiary claim is timing: test scores began declining around 2012, well before COVID-19, which she uses to argue smartphones and later school-issued devices -- not the pandemic alone -- are the primary driver.

Her Common Sense Media citation is a striking concrete data point: a quarter of surveyed teens said they'd seen pornographic content during the school day, and almost half of that group saw it specifically on a school-issued device.

Cross-national evidence anchors the argument beyond anecdote: her own October 2025 Journal of Adolescence study found countries with more school-day leisure device use saw larger test-score declines, with Finland's steep 2006-2022 drop contrasted against Japan's relative stability.

She identifies a structural problem for parents: districts tell them 'there is no substitute for parental supervision' while simultaneously preventing them from installing parental-control software on school-issued devices -- a policy contradiction she calls out directly.

Her policy recommendations are concrete and actionable rather than merely diagnostic: securely lock down devices, scale back device-dependent assignments, allow opt-outs (citing a pending Vermont bill), and consider device-free models in lower grades.
quotes: The standardized test scores of American students had been rising for decades. Then they began to slide, dropping to their lowest point in two decades in 2023 and 2024.
The decline in test scores started well before the pandemic, around 2012. One obvious culprit is smartphones, which became popular just as test scores started to decline.

Sylvie McNamara, a parent of a ninth grader in Washington, D.C., wrote in Washingtonian magazine that her son was spending every class period watching TV shows and playing games on his school-issued laptop.

In a survey of American teenagers by the nonprofit Common Sense Media, one-fourth admitted they had seen pornographic content during the school day. Almost half of that group saw it on a school-issued device.
The more time college students spent doing something else on their laptops during class, the lower their exam scores, even after accounting for academic ability.

In 2022, teenagers in Finland admitted to using their devices during the school day for noneducational purposes for nearly 90 minutes. Perhaps as a result, the test scores of Finnish students plummeted between 2006 and 2022.
Although it once seemed like a good idea to give every child his or her own device, it’s clear that those policies have been a failure.
